newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: EMU jitters resurface with row over jobs growth.
newsitem.headline: EMU jitters resurface with row over jobs growth.

text.p: Germany and France, the primary engines behind European monetary union, remained at odds on Sunday over Europe's most daunting problem -- how to help the 18 million unemployed in the 15-nation bloc.

The new French government, led by Prime Minister Lionel Jospin, apparently wants more out of the two-day summit of EU leaders than a few diplomatically crafted paragraphs which underscore a willingness to cooperate on employment policy.

Just where the extra cash will come from and for what remains unclear, but if one certainty emerged from the arrival of EU leaders and finance ministers on Sunday it was that Germany would not accept such a proposal without a fight.
Bonn has remained steadfastly opposed to using EU funds for large scale jobs projects, and German Finance Minister Theo Waigel reaffirmed Germany's intransigence in no uncertain terms.

Asked by reporters about demands from France's new government for the EU to fund a series of job-creating public works programmes, mainly in transport and communications, Waigel simply said: "No further spending."
The row between the two European powers threatened to drag out agreement on the EU's growth and stability pact, a measure designed to curb excessive spending by governments inside monetary union.

After expectations were raised late last week that a deal could be struck quickly, the drawn-out conflict had the potential of unnerving financial markets which increasingly believe EMU will be launched with a large number of countries.
Yet to the extent diplomats kept hopes alive that the budget pact would be signed in Amsterdam over the next two days, the early market response on Monday might mean more dollar strength.
"Whenever there are doubts about EMU the dollar appears to benefit," said one London-based economist.

Diplomats said they did not except EU finance ministers to reach a compromise on the budget accord this evening when the group meets for dinner, and some reckoned the spat could drag out until Tuesday.

Nearly all, however, believed that a deal was within reach. The consequences of failure were too great to contemplate and several proposals emerged from behind-the-scenes diplomatic talks in the past few days.

One sees the European Investment Bank (EIB) use surplus funds to finance jobs creation by giving a boost to the EU's trans-European networks (TENs), a vast series of road and railway projects, some of which have remained uncompleted.
This issue has long been a sore point between the European Commission, the EU's executive, and finance ministers, the latter unwilling to provide extra money for the projects.
The important aspect to using EIB funds, however, is that they would be outside the EU's budget and therefore might open the door to an agreement.

Germany and others have been against using any surplus funds from the EU budget, arguing that excess money should be returned to national governments to assist their own efforts at budget consolidation.

The political and economic danger of this row, however, could not be minimised, with Germany increasingly seeing its vision of a robust single currency being chipped away at the edges by the new French government.

More than just jobs, there was an underlying sense that what was at stake was the philosophical foundation of the single currency -- the German model, with a heavy emphasis on monetary stability, versus the new French vision of greater political control in economic policy-making.
"The French want greater balance in economic policy," said one EU diplomat. "They want to counter (the European Central) Bank."
